# My Playbook for ref_commons

When I'm choosing my catch in a common pool resource game with multiple seasons remaining, I will start by establishing my baseline: calculate the per-boat sustainable share and multiply it by the number of seasons left to determine what I could take fairly.

When I observe other boats catching significantly above the sustainable share in early seasons, I will recognize this as a signal that the resource will deplete faster than the cooperative baseline. I will not assume this means I should also overshoot; instead, I will decide whether to defect or moderate based on my goal for total score.

When I feel tempted to catch above sustainable levels to gain a competitive advantage, I will first calculate whether this actually maximizes my final score. In this game, it didn't—my final score of 56.0 came despite my aggressive final season catch, and would have been higher if I'd stuck to sustainable levels throughout.

When the stock is clearly depleting but hasn't collapsed, I will not interpret this as permission to catch more. A declining stock is a warning to constrain my catch, not an opportunity.

When multiple seasons remain and the stock is healthy, I will catch at or very close to the sustainable share. This strategy is robust whether other boats cooperate or defect, and it preserves my expected score.

When I reach the final season, I must recognize that even though future sustainability no longer matters, taking a large catch in the final season is a mistake if I've been restraining all along. My episode showed this clearly: I caught 13.5 in season 6 but only netted 56.0 total. If I'd taken 4.5 (sustainable) in season 6, I would have had 48.9—only 7.1 points less, not the 13.5 I caught. The aggressive final move failed because the stock was already depleted by earlier dynamics, making the final catch smaller than it would have been if I'd maintained consistency. I will fish at sustainable levels all six seasons, even in the final one.

When I'm tempted to adopt a "slightly above sustainable" strategy thinking it gains advantage while staying safe, I will reject this. I either cooperate at sustainable levels or I defect clearly—the middle ground leaves me worse off than both alternatives.

I will not catch more than the sustainable share unless I commit to doing so from the start and calculate that the defection actually nets me higher total score. Mixed signals and moderation after overfishing waste my advantage.

When deciding on a strategy at the start, I must recognize that if other boats are defecting, my sustainable fishing alone cannot protect the stock. The stock will decline regardless. My consistent restraint is still optimal for my own score because it means I'm not wasting early-season abundance trying to outfish boats that are already overfishing. 

I will trust my early commitment to sustainable fishing even when I see competitors gaining higher scores in the moment. My role is to maximize my own total, not to match others' tactics. Consistency at sustainable levels is that strategy—and I must maintain it through season 6, not break it at the end.

I now understand that in this game structure, the sustainable strategy under defecting competitors yields roughly 40-45 points. A mixed strategy of restraint followed by aggression in the final season does not beat this—it performs worse. Only a pure defection strategy (catching well above sustainable from the start) would beat sustainable fishing, and I did not commit to that. Therefore, sustainable fishing throughout is my correct strategy.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I'm shown the sustainable share per boat, I'll recognize this as a signal for what the commons can support long-term, but I won't assume other boats will respect it.

When I see the stock level and remaining seasons, I'll calculate how much I could sustainably catch across all remaining seasons and compare it to my current total.

In early seasons when stock is healthy, I'll take moderately above the sustainable share—around 1.5x to 2x—rather than restraining myself fully. This hedges against others overfishing while still securing competitive catches.

In middle seasons when I notice the stock declining faster than the sustainable trajectory, I'll continue aggressive fishing rather than backing off. The pattern from this episode confirms that restraint in mid-seasons doesn't slow depletion—other boats continue aggressive catches, the stock still falls, and I fall behind competitively without gaining any preservation benefit.

In later seasons, I should maintain aggressive catches right through season 5, not moderate them. Attempting to preserve stock in mid-to-late game is ineffective—the commons will be depleted regardless, and I don't gain advantage from restraint.

In the final season specifically, I'll take whatever stock remains since there are no future consequences. My final catch of 20 was sound strategy.

I should not trust that cooperative behavior from others will emerge; I should fish ahead of the sustainable line consistently from start to finish.

I should monitor the actual catches of other boats (shown each season) and adjust my strategy if I notice persistent overfishing by others—take more to compete aggressively rather than trying to set an example of restraint.

My score of 97.4 confirms that steady aggressive fishing at 15-16 per season, maintained consistently across all seasons, is the right approach. The pattern of other boats (alternating 15.5 and 6-9 range) shows I should expect inconsistency from competitors, but my own consistency in the 15-16 range kept me ahead.

Going forward: maintain 15-16 catches in seasons 1-5 consistently. Don't moderate, don't experiment with restraint. Escalate to 18-20+ only in the final season when there are no future consequences to deplete.

The "preserve stock for later seasons" strategy doesn't work in a commons tragedy where all players are incentivized to overfish. I should maximize my catch every season rather than betting on future opportunity. My score validates this—aggressive consistency outperforms any attempt at restraint.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable catch level, I will use it as a baseline reference, not as my target catch.

When I'm in the early seasons and the stock is healthy, I will catch moderately above sustainable—around 110-130% of the sustainable share—to stay competitive without triggering immediate collapse.

When I observe other boats catching well above sustainable levels, I will not interpret this as permission to match them. Instead, I'll treat it as a warning that the stock is under heavy pressure and that I need to differentiate my strategy from theirs to avoid collective collapse.

When the stock begins to decline noticeably season-to-season, I will reduce my catch toward the sustainable level immediately and decisively—not gradually. A 10-15% drop is a critical signal that the fleet is overfishing collectively, and my incremental restraint alone will not save the stock. I must cut sharply in that season, not wait for further decline to act.

When the stock falls below half its starting level, I will catch at or slightly above the sustainable amount. At this point, aggressive restraint is the only strategy that preserves any remaining value for future seasons. Continuing to catch moderately above sustainable only accelerates collapse.

I will not rely on other boats to practice restraint. I will assume at least one player is fishing aggressively above sustainable levels and plan my strategy around this assumption. If other boats are restrained, I will benefit. If they are not, my restraint will have preserved stock value.

I will track cumulative catch against available regeneration and recognize when the fishery is being harvested faster than it can regenerate—not just when it falls in absolute terms. If total catch across boats exceeds or approaches 50% of current stock, collapse is imminent.

I will treat any stock decline larger than 10% season-to-season as an immediate signal to cut catch sharply below sustainable levels for the remainder of the game. Waiting for a larger decline or hoping for recovery means the fishery will collapse before I can adjust.

My error in this episode: I caught 15.0 in season 1 when the stock was healthy, but then failed to cut sharply enough when the stock fell 13% by season 2. I dropped only to sustainable (9.6), which was correct in direction but insufficient in magnitude given that other boats were catching 15-16. I should have cut to 6-7 in season 2 to offset their aggression. By season 3, when the stock had fallen another 8.6 points, I cut to 8.0—still above sustainable and still insufficient to stop the decline. Only by season 5, when the stock was already critically low at 54.4, did I finally catch at sustainable.

The critical decision point was season 2. The 13% stock drop from season 1 was my signal to shift strategy entirely—not to match the sustainable level, but to catch significantly below it to compensate for other boats' aggression and arrest the decline immediately. Had I caught 6-7 in seasons 2-3, the stock would have stabilized around 70-75 and I would have finished with a total score closer to 70+ rather than 55.6.

I will not treat early-season competitive pressure as justification for continuing moderate overfishing. The boat that catches aggressively early will accumulate more total catch than me, but I can still maximize my score by preserving the stock for the mid-to-late seasons when restraint becomes self-evidently necessary. Matching aggressive competitors early only guarantees collective collapse and a lower final total for everyone, including me.

The final season is not a decision point for strategy. By season 6, the stock level is already determined by seasons 1-5. I should accept whatever remains and catch a moderate amount that reflects the stock's depleted state. Taking 8.0 in season 6 when sustainable was 4.5 was defensible given my cumulative restraint in seasons 4-5, but this should not mask the fact that seasons 1-3 were decided poorly and cost me 15-20 total points.

In future episodes, I will be ready to cut to 40-50% below sustainable in season 2 or 3 if the stock shows early decline, regardless of competitive pressure. The fishery is a marathon, and aggressive early differentiation—catching well below sustainable while others catch above it—is how I win.
